newsitem.title: INDIA: More rises seen as India stocks scale 33-month peak.
newsitem.headline: More rises seen as India stocks scale 33-month peak.

text.p: Indian stocks broke through a 33-month-old peak on Wednesday, propelled by falling interest rates, and analysts expect the market to continue pushing towards a record high.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-share index hit 4,395.31 points in afternoon trade, exceeding the 4,386.43 level reached on October 14, 1994.
"There might be a short-term melt-down but the market has more to go," said Bharat Iyer, strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
"We're maintaining our target of 4,600-4,700 by December 1997," he said.
That would bring the index into the territory of an all-time high of 4,643.31 reached on September 12, 1994.
Peregrine Capital has set a slightly less ambitious year-end target of 4,500.

The market has been bolstered by hefty cash inflows by domestic and foreign investors along with a shift of local money into equities from fixed income instruments following a slide in interest rates, analysts said.
Since April 1, the central bank's key bank rate has dropped by two percentage points to 10 percent.
"Funds should ideally flow into equities when interest rates start falling," said Deepak Mehta, equities trader at Reliance Capital Ltd. "This is exactly what's happening."
After a two-year bear phase, Indian markets were now attracting foreign funds, especially when compared to other emerging markets, the analysts said.
"India is relatively attractive," said Mihir Doshi, executive director at Morgan Stanley in charge of Indian equity operations. "There's real demand."
Iyer at UBS said foreign funds had been underweight in Indian stocks but were changing that weighting partly in response to better earnings expected for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March).

He said Indian stocks were projected to produce earnings growth of 20 percent in 1997/98. At a price-earnings multiple of about 14, based on prospective earnings, the market remained very attractive, he added.

Data so far have not indicated an economic upturn but lower rates and a drop in individual taxes -- the 1997/98 budget cut the maximum personal taxes to 30 percent from 40 percent -- are expected to spur demand.
R. Ramakrishnan, chief dealer at broker ASK Raymond James Securities, said lower interest rates should boost the bottom line of companies this year.
